name: Masstree
workload: 20M key-value pairs, 16 cores: uniform-key get/put (1-10 byte decimal keys, 8-byte values) and YCSB-derived MYCSB get/put/getrange workloads with Zipfian key popularity, run against 16 Redis processes and 16 memcached processes
claimed_speedup: Uniform get: Masstree 9.10M ops/s vs Redis 5.97M (Redis at 65.6% of Masstree, i.e. Masstree ~1.5x). Uniform put: 5.84M vs 2.97M (50.9%, ~2.0x). MYCSB-C all-get: 9.86M vs Redis 2.70M (27.4%, ~3.65x) and vs memcached 5.28M (53.6%, ~1.87x). Paper states Masstree 'outperforms the other systems on almost all workloads, usually by a substantial margin,' with the single exception that memcached is 7.4% faster than Masstree on the uniform get workload.
hardware: 48-core server: eight 2.4 GHz six-core AMD Opteron 8431 chips, Linux 3.1.5
tradeoffs: Masstree is a research B+-tree/trie key-value engine, not a drop-in Redis replacement: no rich data types (columns emulated via byte-range reads/writes on values), manual client-side sharding across processes/threads, and the same paper shows a plain partitioned hash table (memcached, single core) can beat Masstree by ~2.5x on pure uniform gets.
caveats: Numbers are from the original authors' own EuroSys 2012 paper ('Cache Craftiness for Fast Multicore Key-Value Storage', Mao/Kohler/Morris), not an independent third party; hardware is a 2012-era 48-core AMD Opteron machine so results may not transfer to modern CPUs; compiler and optimization flags are not stated anywhere in the paper (tier capped below A for this reason); GitHub shows no explicit OSI license file (license field is NOASSERTION).
found_via: Blogs/talks: highscalability.com post 'Masstree - Much Faster than MongoDB, VoltDB, Redis, and Competitive with Memcached' (surfaced via HN Algolia query 'faster than memcached', title also matched seed query intent 'faster than Redis benchmark engineering blog'), linking to the EuroSys 2012 paper and github.com/kohler/masstree-beta

name: Ristretto
baseline: LRU (plain mutex-protected LRU cache using golang/groupcache/lru, labeled as a baseline implementation in the benchmark suite)
workload: Concurrent Get/Set operations (mixed, read, write) under Zipfian key popularity, plus hit-ratio traces (ARC search/database, LIRS looping, CODASYL), benchmarked in dgraph-io/dgraph-benchmarks' cachebench suite against a mutex-protected LRU cache and other Go cache libraries (BigCache, FreeCache, FastCache, Goburrow)
claimed_speedup: README and linked benchmark charts (Throughput - Mixed/Read/Write, Hit Ratios - Search/Database/Looping/CODASYL, all SVGs in the ristretto repo) claim Ristretto has 'best in class' hit ratios ('on par with exact LRU and better performance on Search and Database traces') and the highest concurrent throughput of the caches tested; the charts are unlabeled (no numeric axis text extractable), so no specific x-factor is stated as text.
stars_or_usage: 6,994 stars; used in Dgraph and Badger
tradeoffs: Ristretto is an embedded in-process Go library, not a networked cache server, so it is not directly comparable to Redis/memcached on a fair basis (no network I/O); SampledLFU/TinyLFU admission adds CPU overhead per operation in exchange for hit-ratio gains; benchmark 'ratio' figures (e.g. 0.18%-98.99% hit rate rows in the README example output) vary hugely by trace and are workload-dependent.
caveats: This is the project's own benchmark suite (dgraph-io/dgraph-benchmarks); no CPU model or Go build flags are stated on the README or in the linked benchmark directory, and the only quantitative results are baked into unlabeled SVG chart images rather than given as text -- capped at Tier C per the rubric ('project's own benchmark code with partial methodology is C, not B'). The original 'Introducing Ristretto' blog post at blog.dgraph.io/post/introducing-ristretto-high-perf-go-cache/ now returns 404.
found_via: Blogs/talks: Hacker News thread (215 points) 'Ristretto: A High Performance, Concurrent, Memory-Bound Go Cache' linking to the dgraph.io blog post (query variants around 'faster than memcached'/'cache benchmark engineering blog')
